ra: Cordovero led the systematizing school of Kabbalah in 16th-c Safed.
Luria, the Ari, was the central master of the Safed circle.
Vital was a leading member of Luria's Safed circle.
Karo was a pillar of the Safed mystical-halakhic community.
Alkabetz, author of Lekhah Dodi, belonged to the Safed circle.
Luria briefly studied with Cordovero in Safed; his system built upon and superseded Cordovero's.
Vital was Luria's foremost disciple and the recorder of his teachings.
Vital first studied Cordoverian Kabbalah before becoming Luria's disciple.
Alkabetz was Cordovero's teacher and brother-in-law.
Luria taught the doctrine of Tzimtzum, the divine self-contraction.
The Reshimu (residue) is a core element of Luria's cosmogony.
The Kav (ray of light entering the void) is part of Luria's emanation scheme.
Luria taught Shevirat ha-Kelim, the breaking of the vessels.
Luria taught Tikkun, the cosmic restoration.
Olam ha-Tohu, the World of Chaos that shattered, is central to Lurianic cosmology.
The scattered netzotzot (holy sparks) to be raised are a Lurianic doctrine.
Adam Kadmon, the primordial man, is a foundational Lurianic figure.
Luria's partzuf doctrine includes Arikh Anpin (the Long Face).
Atika Kadisha (the Holy Ancient One) is a Lurianic partzuf.
The partzuf Abba (Father) belongs to Luria's configuration of the sefirot.
The partzuf Imma (Mother) belongs to Luria's configuration.
Zeir Anpin (the Small Face) is a central Lurianic partzuf.
Nukva (the Female) is a Lurianic partzuf paired with Zeir Anpin.
Vital transmitted Luria's Tikkun doctrine in Etz Chaim.
Vital recorded the Shevirat ha-Kelim teaching in Etz Chaim.
Luzzatto systematized the Lurianic doctrine of Tikkun for later readers.
Luzzatto's metaphysics centers on the unfolding of the Ein Sof's providence.
Alkabetz's Lekhah Dodi welcomes the Sabbath as the Shekhinah, the divine bride.
Sabbatai Zevi was the messianic figurehead of the Sabbatean movement.
Nathan of Gaza was the prophet-theologian of the Sabbatean movement.
Nathan of Gaza proclaimed Sabbatai Zevi as the messiah and built the theology around him.
Sabbatean messianism interpreted Tikkun and Lurianic redemption as fulfilled in Sabbatai Zevi.
Nathan's theology of the apostasy framed the messiah's descent among the qliphoth to raise the sparks.
The Baal Shem Tov is the founder of the Hasidic movement.
Dov Ber, the Maggid, succeeded the Baal Shem Tov as leader of Hasidism.
Schneur Zalman founded the Chabad branch of Hasidism.
Nachman founded the Breslov branch of Hasidism.
Levi Yitzhak of Berditchev was a leading Hasidic rebbe.
Elimelech of Lizhensk shaped Polish-Galician Hasidism.
Jacob Joseph of Polonne was the first to record the Baal Shem Tov's teachings in print.
Dov Ber was the chief disciple of the Baal Shem Tov.
Jacob Joseph was a direct disciple of the Baal Shem Tov.
Schneur Zalman was a disciple of Dov Ber, the Maggid.
Levi Yitzhak of Berditchev was a disciple of Dov Ber.
Elimelech of Lizhensk was a disciple of Dov Ber.
Nachman of Breslov was the great-grandson of the Baal Shem Tov (descent line, not literal parent).
The Tanya develops a distinctive contemplative reading of the Lurianic Tzimtzum.
Chabad theology centers on the immanence of the Ein Sof within creation.
The Baal Shem Tov popularized the Lurianic raising of holy sparks (netzotzot) in everyday life.
The Vilna Gaon led the Mitnagdim and issued bans against the Hasidic movement.
Chayyim of Volozhin was the foremost disciple of the Vilna Gaon.
Chayyim of Volozhin gave the Mitnagdic opposition to Hasidism its theological framework in Nefesh ha-Chayyim.
The Vilna Gaon was a serious kabbalist who commented on the sefirotic system within the Lithuanian tradition.
